hints: Look closely at where the dark, condensed chromosomes are in the micrograph, are they in the middle or pulled apart to opposite ends?
Think about what separates late anaphase from early telophase, chromosomes at poles versus nuclear envelope reforming and decondensation starting.
walkthrough:
**Observe what you can actually see**

Look at the pale central cell. You can see two dark masses of condensed chromosomes, one at the top left and one at the bottom right.

The cell looks pinched in the middle, but there is no clear cell plate or two separate nuclei yet.

**Recall anaphase versus telophase**

In anaphase, sister chromatids separate and move to opposite poles, so you see two groups of condensed chromosomes.

In telophase, those two groups stay at the poles, but the nuclear envelopes start to reform and chromosomes start to decondense.

**Explain the difficulty**

This micrograph is caught right on the boundary. The chromosomes have reached the poles, so anaphase movement may just be finishing.

But there is no clear new nuclear envelope or decondensation, so we cannot be sure telophase has definitely started. That overlap makes the exact stage hard to name.

options.A: Centrioles are very small and often out of the plane of section in a TEM, so not seeing them does not cause the confusion here.
options.B: The image shows the transition point with chromosomes at opposite poles, so it could be late anaphase still continuing or very early telophase just starting.
options.C: This is not metaphase because chromosomes are not lined up on the equator, they are already separated into two polar groups in one dividing cell.
options.D: Interphase has not started because the chromosomes are still dark, condensed and visible, with no reformed nuclei.
